                     fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%", dpi = 120)

## What you will learn

Binning means replacing a numeric measurement with a category. For example,
instead of keeping someone's exact participation score, you might record
"no participation", "lower participation", or "higher participation".
That can make a distinction easier to communicate. It also discards differences
between people placed in the same group.

`binwise` helps you examine that trade-off. It does not issue a universal verdict
that a variable should be binned. Start with your question, inspect what the
categories would contain, and check the consequences for the analysis you want
to do.

This tutorial uses six small simulated datasets included with the package.
Simulation lets us know the underlying rule in two examples. Real data rarely
give us that advantage. Nothing here needs the author's paper, a downloaded
file, or objects left over from another R session.

**Suggested pace.** Work through sections 1 to 4 first, then take a break.
Sections 5 and 6 compare predictions. Sections 7 and 8 cover negative values
and changes across zero. You can stop after any complete section and return
later by rerunning the earlier code.

| Function | The question it helps answer |
|:--|:--|
| `bin_diagnose()` | What values and observation counts would these bins contain? |
| `bin_compare()` | How do different sets of bins group the same observations? |
| `bin_apply()` | How do I add my chosen categories to my data? |
| `bin_interact()` | How do fitted relationships change when I use categories? |
| `bin_validate()` | How well do the competing models predict held-out observations? |

## 1. Start a clean RStudio session

A **package** is a collection of reusable functions, documentation, and sometimes
datasets. Installing a package puts those files on your computer. Loading it
makes its functions available in the current R session.

This development draft must already be installed from the supplied package
archive or project instructions. It is not currently available through
`install.packages("binwise")`. Once installed in an active library, run this
in RStudio's **Console**.

```{r load-package}
library(binwise)
```

If you use the local development project, open `binwise.Rproj` and run
`source("tools/start.R")` instead. That project helper locates the local
installation and loads it. The rest of this guide is the same for everyone.
You can reopen the installed guide with
`vignette("getting-started", package = "binwise")`.

For a comfortable way to work, choose **File > New File > R Script**, copy one
code block into the script, select it, and press **Command+Enter** on a Mac or
**Ctrl+Enter** on Windows. Run the blocks in order. Results appear in the Console;
figures appear in **Plots**, where **Zoom** makes them larger. Save your script
so you have a record of your steps. You do not need to click Knit to follow this
guide.

A few pieces of R notation will help.

| Notation | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `result <- ...` | Run the expression and save its result under the name `result`. |
| `"score"` | A column name supplied as text. Keep the quotation marks. |
| `result$bins` | Open the component named `bins` inside a saved result. |
| `# a comment` | An explanation that R ignores. |
| `TRUE` and `FALSE` | Turn an option on or off. Capitalization matters. |
| `NA` | A missing value, not the number zero. |

Copy code from the code blocks, not the printed output beneath them. Output lines
beginning with `#>` are shown to help you compare your results. A successful
assignment often prints nothing. Type the saved object's name to inspect it.

## 2. When zero means something different

Imagine a participation score. Zero means that someone did not participate;
a positive number measures how much they participated. That distinction comes
from the meaning of the variable, not from the shape of a histogram.

First, load the example and look at its first six rows. A **data frame** is a
table with observations in rows and variables in columns.

```{r zero-data}
data("binwise_zero", package = "binwise")
head(binwise_zero)
nrow(binwise_zero)
sum(binwise_zero$score == 0)
```

You should see 1,000 rows and 400 exact zeros. `id` identifies an observation;
`score` is the variable we want to inspect. `== 0` checks which scores equal zero,
and `sum()` counts those matches here.

Now ask for three intervals among positive scores and a separate zero category.

```{r zero-diagnosis}
zero_scheme <- bin_diagnose(
  binwise_zero, "score", bins = 3,
  separate_zero = TRUE, warn = FALSE
)
zero_scheme
```

The saved result contains both tables and a plain-language assessment. Here,
`warn = FALSE` keeps advisory messages in the report instead of repeating them as
R warnings. It does not make invalid inputs acceptable.

Look more closely at just the boundaries and counts.

```{r zero-table}
zero_scheme$bins[, c("bin", "lower", "upper", "n", "proportion")]
```

`n` is the number of observations in a category. `proportion` is its share of
usable observations, so `0.4` means 40%. `lower` and `upper` describe interval
boundaries. There are **four categories**, because `bins = 3` requests three
positive intervals in addition to the zero category. The counts are 400, 200,
200, and 200.

**What should you conclude?** Keeping nonparticipation separate makes sense for
this fictional question. There is no reason yet to conclude that the positive
scores also need three categories. You could instead use a zero indicator and
retain positive intensity as a continuous measurement. Describing a meaningful
zero is a different decision from categorizing every positive value.

The automatic zero option currently requires nonnegative values. Section 8
shows how to handle a boundary at zero when negative values also occur.

## 3. Create a categorical variable while keeping the original

A **scheme** is a saved set of boundaries and assignment rules. Once you choose
one, `bin_apply()` uses those same rules to create a **factor**, R's representation
of a categorical variable.

```{r apply-zero}
participation <- bin_apply(
  binwise_zero, zero_scheme, name = "participation_group"
)
head(participation)
table(participation$participation_group)
is.factor(participation$participation_group)
```

`participation` is a new data frame. It contains the original `score` column and
the new `participation_group` column. The last line prints `TRUE`.
You have now created a variable you can use in tables or models. You have not
changed the original `binwise_zero` dataset.

The factor is not the same as assigning the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 and treating
them as a numeric measurement. A model using a factor can estimate separate
category differences without assuming equal distances between categories.

Saved schemes are also useful for applying consistent definitions to new data.
Values beyond a scheme's saved finite range produce an error by default.
`out_of_range = "NA"` explicitly marks those values missing instead. Investigate
such values rather than silently dropping them. For prediction evaluation,
use the training-only recipes shown in section 6.

## 4. When balanced counts hide a long upper tail

A **quantile** scheme aims for similar numbers of observations in each bin.
Four quantile bins are commonly called quartiles. An **equal-width** scheme
divides the numeric range into equally wide intervals. These are different
objectives, and neither guarantees useful categories.

```{r tail-comparison}
data("binwise_tail", package = "binwise")
tail_comparison <- bin_compare(binwise_tail, "share", bins = 4)
plot(
  tail_comparison, type = "boundaries", show_counts = TRUE,
  value_format = "percent", xlab = "Share", main = "Counts and ranges tell different stories",
  scheme_labels = c(quantile_4 = "Four quantile bins",
                    equal_width_4 = "Four equal-width bins")
)
```

The variable is stored as a fraction between 0 and 1. Percentage formatting
makes `0.01` appear as 1%; it does not change the data or boundaries.
For variables already stored from 0 to 100, use `percent_scale = 1`.
For income, temperature, or other measurements, leave out percentage formatting.

**Read the picture in two passes.** First, examine each horizontal interval.
A long interval means that very different numeric values are assigned to the
same category. Second, read `n` beside each interval. That is its observation
count. A narrow interval can contain many observations; a wide interval can
contain very few. Open and filled endpoints show excluded and included bounds.
By default, intervals include their upper endpoint and the first interval also
includes its lower endpoint. Displayed cutpoints are rounded; saved boundaries
retain their precision.

Orange marks indicate categories below the chosen screening thresholds. The
defaults are 20 observations or 1% of usable observations. These are prompts to
inspect support, not universal rules for statistical adequacy. Row counts are
not necessarily counts of independent people or countries.

For the numerical detail, run this.

```{r tail-table}
tail_comparison$bins[, c("scheme", "bin", "lower", "upper", "n")]
```

**What should you conclude?** The upper quantile bin covers a broad range, while
equal-width bins put most observations in the lowest interval. This identifies
what each choice hides. Skewness alone does not establish that binning will
improve an outcome model. A transformed or flexible continuous predictor may
retain useful information.

You can supply your own thresholds. The following 1%, 5%, and 20% boundaries
are illustrative, not recommendations for every proportion.

```{r custom-tail}
tail_custom <- bin_compare(
  binwise_tail, "share", methods = "quantile",
  custom_breaks = list(chosen_thresholds = c(0, .01, .05, .20, 1))
)
tail_custom$bins[, c("scheme", "bin", "lower", "upper", "n")]
share_data <- bin_apply(
  binwise_tail, tail_custom$diagnoses$chosen_thresholds, name = "share_group"
)
```

Use thresholds motivated by your question and inspect their counts. A custom
scheme is an option you can evaluate, not a claim that those boundaries are true.

## 5. A case where bins discard a useful relationship

Now add an **outcome**, the quantity we want to explain or predict. In this
simulation, its expected value increases smoothly with exposure. There is no
threshold. Random noise makes individual observations scatter around that rule.

```{r smooth-data}
data("binwise_smooth", package = "binwise")
plot(binwise_smooth$exposure, binwise_smooth$outcome,
     pch = 16, cex = .45, col = "grey65",
     xlab = "Exposure", ylab = "Observed outcome")
abline(a = 2, b = .5, col = "#397985", lwd = 2)
```

The line shows the known simulated mean, `2 + 0.5 * exposure`. An additional
10 units of exposure raises that mean by 5 units. The dataset also stores this
rule in `expected_outcome`. That column is a teaching aid, not an extra control
to put in a model of the noisy outcome.

Compare a continuous linear predictor with four quantile categories.

```{r smooth-model}
smooth_scheme <- bin_diagnose(binwise_smooth, "exposure", bins = 4, warn = FALSE)
smooth_fit <- bin_interact(
  binwise_smooth, outcome = "outcome", variables = "exposure",
  schemes = list(quartiles = smooth_scheme)
)
plot(smooth_fit, xlab = "Exposure", ylab = "Predicted mean outcome",
     main = "A smooth relationship becomes steps")
```

Despite its name, `bin_interact()` also works with just one predictor. With a
single variable, it fits no interaction. The continuous model is included
automatically. The model named `quartiles` replaces exposure with the saved
categories.

The continuous line follows a trend. The binned line stays flat within each
interval and jumps at its boundary. Those flat sections assume that exposure
values in the same bin have the same predicted mean, with other predictors
held fixed. They hide changes that matter in this simulation.

The shading shows **95% pointwise confidence intervals for the fitted mean**.
These are model-based intervals conditional on the chosen cutpoints. They are
not intervals containing 95% of individual outcomes, and they do not include
uncertainty from choosing the bins. Bands may be too narrow to see clearly.
Two bands overlapping, or a step crossing a continuous line, does not show that
binning is appropriate or establish that the models are equivalent.

Read the package's assessment with these lines.

```{r smooth-assessment}
cat(paste(smooth_fit$assessment, collapse = "\n\n"))
```

This assessment describes the fitted comparison. It does not know the true
relationship in your own data. In-sample fit is also different from prediction
on observations withheld from fitting.

## 6. Test predictions, then see a case where bins help

### First evaluate the smooth example

**Cross-validation** separates the data into groups called folds. With five
folds, each model fits on four folds and predicts the fifth. Repeating this
process gives each eligible observation a prediction from a model that did not
fit that observation.

For validation, supply a **recipe** describing how to construct bins. Do not
supply `smooth_scheme`, which was calculated using the whole dataset.
The recipe below learns quartile boundaries separately inside each training
sample. `probs` lists cumulative proportions from 0 to 1.

```{r smooth-validation}
smooth_check <- bin_validate(
  binwise_smooth, outcome = "outcome", variables = "exposure",
  schemes = list(quartiles = list(
    exposure = list(probs = c(0, .25, .50, .75, 1))
  )),
  folds = 5, seed = 12, reps = 199
)
smooth_check$scores
smooth_check$differences
```

`seed` makes the random folds and resampling reproducible. `reps = 199` requests
a small number of bootstrap repetitions for this teaching example. For a final
analysis, use more repetitions and check the stability of the intervals.

**Read the scores.** RMSE means root mean squared prediction error; it gives
larger errors extra weight. MAE means mean absolute prediction error. Both are
in the outcome's units, and lower is better. Here, RMSE is about 3.01 for the
continuous model and 4.66 for quartiles. The bins predict worse in this example.

**Read the differences.** A difference is the candidate score minus the
continuous reference score. Positive values favor the reference; negative
values favor the candidate. The paired difference compares predictions for
the same held-out observations.

### Now evaluate a genuine threshold

The next dataset contains two predictors, `x` and `z`, plus a control variable.
An **interaction** means that the relationship involving `x` changes with `z`.
A **control** is another predictor included in every candidate model.

For `threshold_outcome`, the simulation has a real jump at `x = 0`. Think of
`x` as distance from a fictional eligibility cutoff. Within either side,
further changes in `x` do not change the expected outcome when `z` and the
control are fixed. This is a feature of the simulated rule, not a claim about
all real eligibility rules.

```{r threshold-model, fig.height=5.5}
data("binwise_interaction", package = "binwise")
threshold_scheme <- bin_diagnose(
  binwise_interaction, "x", method = "custom",
  breaks = c(min(binwise_interaction$x), 0, max(binwise_interaction$x)),
  warn = FALSE
)
threshold_fit <- bin_interact(
  binwise_interaction, outcome = "threshold_outcome",
  variables = c("x", "z"), controls = "control",
  schemes = list(threshold = threshold_scheme)
)
plot(threshold_fit, xlab = "Distance from the cutoff",
     main = "A known threshold whose size varies with z")
```

There is one panel for each displayed value of `z`. `x` varies along the
horizontal axis, and the control is held fixed. Only `x` is binned; `z` stays
continuous. With two focal variables the interaction is included by default.
To compare additive models instead, set `interaction = FALSE`.

At `z = 0` and `control = 0`, the known mean is 1 for `x <= 0` and 2.8 for
`x > 0`. A continuous linear interaction spreads that jump across the range
of `x`. The threshold model can represent the jump directly.

Now test the threshold without fitting the held-out outcomes.

```{r threshold-validation}
threshold_check <- bin_validate(
  binwise_interaction, outcome = "threshold_outcome",
  variables = c("x", "z"), controls = "control",
  schemes = list(threshold = list(x = list(breaks = c(-Inf, 0, Inf)))),
  folds = 5, seed = 12, reps = 199
)
threshold_check$scores
plot(threshold_check, metric = "RMSE",
     main = "Negative differences favor the threshold model")
```

`-Inf` and `Inf` mean there is no finite outer limit in this validation recipe.
The cutoff remains exactly zero. Unlike learned quantiles, this fixed boundary
was specified as part of the example before examining the outcomes.

Here, RMSE is about 1.34 for the continuous interaction and 1.20 for the
threshold model. The bins help for the relationship we deliberately simulated.
The plot's horizontal interval concerns the **difference in prediction error**,
not a fitted outcome curve. These bootstrap intervals hold the folds and fitted
predictions fixed; they do not capture every source of uncertainty from
refitting or choosing a model.

**Why is this a reasonable use of bins?** There is a meaningful, known boundary;
the generating mean is constant within each side at fixed `z` and control; and
the held-out comparison supports the threshold model over this continuous
linear benchmark. Overlapping fitted lines alone would not supply that evidence.
In real data, subject knowledge supplies the meaning, and validation tests the
predictive consequences. Better prediction does not by itself establish a
causal effect.

### Check that the comparison actually used the intended observations

```{r validation-coverage}
threshold_check$diagnostics
threshold_check$fold_scores
```

`unavailable = 0` means that candidate produced a usable prediction for every
test row in that fold. Read `messages` if it did not. Scores compare the common
usable predictions, so missing predictions can change the population being
scored. `fold_scores` shows whether an overall improvement conceals poor results
in some folds.

These simulations use independent rows. For repeated observations of people,
firms, or countries, use an appropriate `group` column to keep the same unit
out of both training and test sets. The right grouping depends on the intended
prediction task. Standard folds, including user-supplied `fold_id`, train on
all other folds; they are not a forward-only forecasting procedure.

The original `continuous` benchmark is linear regression or logistic regression
with the specified terms. Add `spline_df = 3` to include a flexible continuous
comparator in either `bin_interact()` or `bin_validate()`. In validation,
`reference = "spline"` compares score differences directly with that spline.
The knots are learned from training observations only. Read the separate guide
with `vignette("flexible-continuous", package = "binwise")` for a step-by-step
example showing why bins can beat a straight line but lose to a curve.
Advanced users can supply other models through `fit_predict`; see `?bin_validate`.
If you try many schemes and choose the best on these folds, use a fresh test
set or nested validation to evaluate the chosen procedure honestly.

## 7. Negative values do not require special bins

This example is an index with an arbitrary origin. Four hundred observations
share the value -10. That repeated number has no separate substantive meaning
in the fictional setting.

```{r negative-values}
data("binwise_negative", package = "binwise")
negative_scheme <- bin_diagnose(binwise_negative, "score", bins = 4, warn = FALSE)
shifted_scheme <- bin_diagnose(binwise_negative, "shifted_score", bins = 4, warn = FALSE)
negative_scheme$bins[, c("bin", "lower", "upper", "n")]
identical(negative_scheme$assignments, shifted_scheme$assignments)
```

You should see three intervals containing 500, 250, and 250 observations, even
though you requested four. The package keeps tied values together; it does not
arbitrarily split identical scores to force equal counts.

`shifted_score` is `score + 11`, so every shifted value is positive. The last
line prints `TRUE`: changing the origin did not change the assignments.
Neither negative signs nor repeated values by themselves justify categories.
A repeated measurement may reflect rounding, a measurement limit, or a real
state. Its meaning needs investigation.

## 8. A useful boundary can exist even when nobody equals zero

Here, negative values mean declines and positive values mean increases. No
observation is exactly zero. If the question is about direction, a boundary
at zero is meaningful even though equal-sized groups would be impossible.

```{r mixed-values}
data("binwise_mixed", package = "binwise")
direction_comparison <- bin_compare(
  binwise_mixed, "change", methods = "quantile",
  custom_breaks = list(direction = c(min(binwise_mixed$change), 0,
                                     max(binwise_mixed$change)))
)
plot(direction_comparison, type = "boundaries", show_counts = TRUE,
     xlab = "Change", main = "Balanced counts or a direction boundary",
     scheme_labels = c(quantile_4 = "Four quantile bins",
                       direction = "Boundary at zero"))
direction_data <- bin_apply(
  binwise_mixed, direction_comparison$diagnoses$direction, name = "direction_group"
)
table(direction_data$direction_group)
```

The direction groups contain 700 declines and 300 increases. The third quantile
bin mixes declines with increases. If preserving direction is the purpose,
the unequal groups are more faithful to that purpose. If the size of change
matters, two groups still throw away useful information.

This is a **boundary at zero**, not a **zero-only category**. Intervals include
their upper endpoint, so a future exact zero would join the lower interval.
Call that interval "nonpositive" if zeros can occur. Do not call it strictly
negative without checking the rule.

## What to take back to your own data

| Example | A defensible conclusion | What it does not establish |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Meaningful zero | Preserve the distinction between no participation and some participation. | All positive values need bins. |
| Long positive tail | Compare counts with ranges before grouping very different values. | Skewness requires categorization. |
| Smooth outcome | Coarse steps lose a useful within-bin trend here. | Bins are never useful for descriptive tables. |
| Known threshold | Prespecified categories can represent a real jump and predict well. | Every apparent bend in a real plot is a threshold. |
| Negative index | Preserve ties and interpret the scale's origin. | Negative values need different statistical treatment simply because of their sign. |
| Mixed-sign changes | A zero boundary can preserve direction with unequal counts. | Direction categories preserve magnitude. |

Before choosing bins, write down their purpose, the meaning of the boundaries,
and what differences you are willing to hide within a category. Report counts
and ranges. Keep the original numeric variable. If prediction matters, evaluate
on held-out data with an appropriate continuous alternative. If interpretation
or causal inference matters, prediction scores alone cannot resolve the choice.

## Common stumbling blocks

| What you see | What to do |
|:--|:--|
| `there is no package called 'binwise'` | Follow the supplied archive installation instructions, or open the local project and run `source("tools/start.R")`. |
| `object ... not found` | Run the earlier block that creates that object, including the relevant `data()` call. |
| `could not find function` | Load `binwise` again after restarting R. |
| A `+` prompt instead of `>` | R is waiting for a closing quote or parenthesis. Press Escape and rerun the complete block. |
| Fewer bins than requested | Check ties and repeated cutpoints in the diagnosis. Equal values stay together. |
| An unreadable plot | Use Plots > Zoom, or enlarge the pane and rerun `plot()`. |
| A boundary appears rounded to zero | Inspect `$bins` with more digits. Display rounding does not change the stored cutoff. |
| Missing rows in model comparisons | Check missing values in every outcome, predictor, and control, plus validation diagnostics. |

Use `?bin_diagnose`, `?bin_apply`, or `?bin_validate` to open detailed help.
For real data and a short guide to related methods and research, open
`vignette("real-data-and-related-work", package = "binwise")`.
